title: admission-control-batch-shaping-playbook
content:
Status: working notes / experimental playbook
Owner: Ayesha Patel (eng-serving-runtime)
Purpose: capture experiments that evaluate admission-control shaped batching as an alternative to pure timeout/size-driven coalescing. Goal is to reduce P99 tail latency for soft-real-time interactive workloads while preserving throughput and per-customer fairness.

Background / motivation:
- Continuous batching has been effective at improving GPU utilization, but tail latency spikes persist during microbursts and when long requests occupy KV cache or GPU context.
- Classic knobs: max_batch_size, max_wait_ms (timeout), and priority queues. These interact nonlinearly; naive tuning trades off throughput for tail.
- Hypothesis: admitting requests based on an admission score (estimated remaining tokens, customer weight, age) and shaping them into batches before enqueue gives finer control over tail and fairness than only timeouts.

Key ideas explored in this doc (novel elements):
1) Token-shaped admission: estimate "tokens remaining" using client-supplied prompt_length_hint + mean generation length for model version. Prefer admitting shorter expected-response requests for fast-path coalescing.
2) Soft-fairness with decay: maintain per-customer admission weight that decays exponentially; heavier spenders get momentary demotion to prevent starvation of low-volume customers.
3) Burstlet shaping: hold a micro-buffer (5-20ms window) that preferentially groups similar token-length requests to avoid KV-cache thrash from mixing long and short seqs.
4) Backpressure-aware flush: if GPU queue depth is high, trigger aggressive admission filtering to preserve latency SLOs for high-priority routes.

Experiment matrix (configs):
- Base (control): max_batch_size=64, max_wait_ms=30, fairness=none.
- A1: admission_score = priority - 0.5*est_tokens, soft_fairness_decay=0.1, micro_buffer_ms=10
- A2: admission_score = priority - est_tokens, soft_fairness_decay=0.3, micro_buffer_ms=5
- B1: A1 + aggressive backpressure threshold (GPU_queue_len>12 triggers drop from admission)
- C1: Token-shape-only (no fairness), micro_buffer_ms=15
- D1: Size-first baseline (prefer fill to 64 before timeout) for contrast

Measurement plan / metrics collected:
- Per-experiment 6hr run under synthetic replayed production traces (mixed latency-sensitive chat + batch generation):
  - P50/P95/P99 latency for route-level and global
  - Token throughput TPU-equivalent tokens/s and GPU utilization
  - Batch size distribution (histogram of batch sizes and seq-length variance within batches)
  - Fairness metrics: median latency per-customer quintile, and weighted Jain's index over 1hr windows
  - Regression signals: failure rate, OOMs, model-serving stalls
  - Profiling traces: scheduler queue times, admission evaluation time, kernel launch times, KV cache miss rate

Profiling hooks added for these runs:
- Trace points: admit_start, admit_done, queue_enqueue, queue_dequeue, batch_flush, kernel_start, kernel_end, response_send.
- Lightweight per-request tag includes: route, customer_id_hash, est_tokens, priority, admission_score.
- Aggregation script: scripts/analysis/admission_playbook/aggregate.py (PR referenced above).

Initial run results (summary, 2026-02-20 dry runs):
- Control: P99 = 480ms; P95 = 220ms; throughput = 8.2k tokens/s; batch median = 42. Long-short mix caused high seq-length variance per batch (~std 120 tokens).
- A1: P99 = 320ms (-33%), P95 = 190ms (-14%), throughput = 7.9k tokens/s (-3.7%). Batch median = 30, seq-length variance reduced by 28%. Fairness: top-10% customers saw +6% median latency, bottom 50% saw -12% median latency.
- A2: P99 = 300ms (-37%), P95 = 175ms (-20%), throughput = 7.4k tokens/s (-9.8%). Observed improved tails but slightly lower throughput; some small customers (very low volume) saw variance spikes due to aggressive decay.
- B1: under synthetic burst spike, B1 preserved P99 ~340ms while control spiked to 620ms. Indicates backpressure gating helps during overloaded windows.
- C1: token-shape-only reduced seq-length variance but produced fairness regressions; no decay meant heavy customers dominated buffer and experienced lower p50 but higher p99 across system.

Notable profiling observations:
- Admission evaluation added ~0.4-0.8us/request overhead (negligible compared to wait_ms), but batching logic increased enqueue/dequeue complexity and caused more lock contention in the naive implementation.
- KV cache misses decreased in A1/A2 runs by ~18% because batches had more similar seq lengths and model states. This correlates with lower P99.
- Kernel launch jitter still dominates tail when batches contain long-running sequences; shaping helps but does not eliminate outliers caused by stray requests with huge generation budgets.

Open issues / risks:
- Customer-supplied prompt_length_hint can be noisy/adversarial; need fallback estimator or trimming policy.
- Fairness decay parameters sensitive: too aggressive penalizes high-value customers and can breach contractual SLAs. Need policy binding to customer tier metadata.
- Locking/contended code path in admission/queue must be reworked (lock-free or sharded) before rollout.
- Observed a rare mem-growth when micro_buffer_ms > 20ms under duplicated request patterns; suspected leak in temporary buffer handling.

Next experiments (planned):
1) Sharded admission queues per-cpu core to reduce contention; repeat A1 at scale.
2) Conservative estimator for est_tokens based on 90th percentiles per-route instead of mean. Evaluate resilience to adversarial hints.
3) Tier-aware decay: tie decay factor to customer_tier (enterprise vs self-serve). Run contract-risk analysis.
4) Add synthetic "monster request" detector: pre-check for requests with requested_max_tokens>2048 and route them to separate long-pool with dedicated GPU slots. Measure overall P99 change.
5) A/B test in a small customer subset on Dedicated cluster to observe real-world behavior.

Action items (owners):
- Ayesha: spin up sharded admission prototype (P0) and open PR for lock-free queue changes (target: 2026-03-10).
- Jun: build estimator fallback based on historical route stats; add integration tests for adversarial hints (target: 2026-03-05).
- Elena: run contract risk spreadsheet mapping decay settings to SLA tiers and produce recommended defaults (target: 2026-03-08).
- Noah: investigate memory leak with micro_buffer_ms>20ms, attach heap snapshots and file bug (target: 2026-03-02).

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intentionally pragmatic / messy — experiments are evolving. Please focus reviews on: fairness policy language (Elena), admission metric tradeoffs (Jun), and data-structure contention (Noah).
- Slack thread: #serving-scheduler (see pinned message on 2026-02-21)

Appendix (raw numbers snapshot):
- Control: P50 65ms, P95 220ms, P99 480ms, throughput 8200 tok/s, batches: mean 40, std batch seq-length 120
- A1: P50 68ms, P95 190ms, P99 320ms, throughput 7900 tok/s, batches: mean 30, std seq-length 86
- A2: P50 72ms, P95 175ms, P99 300ms, throughput 7400 tok/s, batches mean 28, std seq-length 70
- B1 (burst window): control P99 620ms -> B1 P99 340ms

References / inspiration:
- prior experiments: queue-hysteresis-fairness-census-and-cohorting-wip.json (see historical results)
- related PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/987

End of doc.
